articles.title: Wild report claims Apple might launch an M5 Ultra MacBook Pro
articles.subtitle: Macworld Reports about Apple switching its MacBooks and iPads to OLED displays have been circulating in the rumor mill for some time now.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Reports about Apple switching its MacBooks and iPads to OLED displays have been circulating in the rumor mill for some time now. A new report by Omdia gives us a more concrete look at when the switch could actually happen, as well as a few far-out details about Apple’s alleged plans. [Omdia appears to have removed the report from its website.]

The first MacBook equipped with an OLED display will reportedly be available “by the end of 2026,” according to the site, which is in line with previous rumors. The MacBook Omdia is referring to is likely to be Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro, which is expected later this year or in early 2027.

It appears, however, that the touchscreen MacBook will be a new addition to the MacBook Pro lineup, a higher-end model that could fall under Apple’s Ultra branding. Omdia states that “the existing 14.3-inch and 16.3-inch MacBook Pro models with LCD + Mini LED backlighting will not be discontinued,” which means the MacBook Pro lineup, as it is now, will continue, with Apple upgrading the chip on a regular basis.

Surprisingly, and perhaps unbelievably, Omdia predicts that this new model is “highly likely to be equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.” Apple’s M5 ultra chip is only used in the Mac Studio, which includes a complex thermal cooling system with a heavy copper heat sink that adds two pounds to the machine’s weight.

Omdia also reports that the MacBook Air will continue to use an LCD display, and that there’s a “new 13.8-inch MacBook, which is expected to launch in 2029 with a hybrid OLED display.” This “new” MacBook is likely an upgraded version of the MacBook Air, which has been reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman to be making the switch to OLED in the future.

Omida also confirms previous reports that an OLED iPad mini will arrive later this year. The current LCD iPad mini was released in October 2024, so it’s due for an update. It would be Apple’s first non-Pro tablet to have an OLED display.

articles.title: Star Wars Zero Company: The Kotaku Review
articles.subtitle: Let’s just get this out of the way right at the beginning. Yes, EA and Bit Reactor’s new tactical Star Wars game, Star Wars Zero Company, plays and looks a lot like a modern XCOM game.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Let’s just get this out of the way right at the beginning. Yes, EA and Bit Reactor’s new tactical Star Wars game, Star Wars Zero Company, plays and looks a lot like a modern XCOM game. It’s impossible to ignore the similarities, and considering the studio was founded by XCOM art director Greg Foertsch, it isn’t a mistake. There’s no debate about it: This is a team building an XCOM game but set in the Star Wars universe.

The question really is: Does Star Wars Zero Company feel like its own thing inspired by the past, or is it just a lesser reskin of a popular tactical strategy game? Thankfully, after playing nearly 30 hours of Zero Company and finishing the game, I can confirm Bit Reactor has made something special that takes advantage of the Star Wars universe to create a game far more impressive than a simple imposter.

Just be prepared for some janky cameras, weird pauses during combat, and graphical oddities.

Heroes on both sides

Star Wars Zero Company, out now on consoles and PC, is set during the final months of the Clone Wars. This is a time period seen during the prequel films as well as the Clone Wars TV series, both of which get referenced many, many times during the game. In Zero Company, you take on the role of Hawks, a former Republic captain who was kicked out after a mission during the war went bad.

Now he runs a small mercenary outfit with his Togruta second-in-command Runa, injured Clone soldier Trick, old friend and former alien boxer Kabbney Uppercut, and Lesat smuggler Neesh. (Hawks can also be a woman, and can belong to an assortment of Star Wars species. )

Things aren’t going well for them at the start of the game, so Hawks and Zero Company end up agreeing to work with the Republic covertly to take on a growing cult of creepy people led by a woman named Fathom who seems to have an unnatural ability to control her followers and others.

Over the next 20+ hours, Zero Company tells one heck of a good Star Wars story, one which rivals most of the recent live-action productions in terms of writing, pacing, and just feeling like good ol’ Star Wars. You got twists, turns, meaningful cameos from characters like Anakin Skywalker, and so much more that I won’t spoil here because I truly don’t want to ruin it for anyone.

What I will say is that by the end of Zero Company, I was sad it was ending even though its finale felt perfect.

What made it so hard to stop playing Zero Company were the interactions between my crew and the relationships that developed over the course of the game. By the end, Hawks ends up recruiting former Separatists, Republic clones, criminals, Jedi, and bounty hunters. How they interact with each other between missions made returning to base so much fun. And there’s a ton of dialogue in this game.

I rarely heard the same line twice and learned so much about each operator. Z ero Company even rewards you for chatting with your crew and includes a mechanic dedicated to tracking how well everyone is getting along or how much they hate each other, which might sway your choice when forced into a tricky situation.

A great example of this is the relationship between Trick and an Umbaran sniper named Luco. These are two people who fought each other in the Clone Wars on a planet with some of the worst, bloodiest battles in the war. Watching that relationship play out, knowing that any character in the game can be permanently killed, really blew me away.

A lot of work went into cutscenes and writing that some players won’t see simply because they fucked up during a battle and lost a good soldier or friend.

War does not make one great

When not hanging out with your crew, you’ll be out on various planets fighting enemies, including droids, cultists, and hired guns. And it’s here that Star Wars Zero Company feels the most like XCOM, but in a good way.

You’re able to bring in up to four squad members on each mission. Each character has a different role, like sniper or medic or gunslinger, which grants them abilities and bonuses. Once you’ve selected a crew and made sure they have some gear and weapon mods, one of two things will then happen.

About 80 percent of the time you’ll land on the planet and immediately be in a fight. Each operator on your squad has three action points, which limits how far they can move, how much they can attack, and what else they can do each turn.

The other 20 percent of the time, you’ll first walk around a planet or city in third-person as Hawks in segments that feel superfluous and not needed. There’s really only one mission that takes advantage of this third-person exploration mode. The rest just feel like a waste of time. Characters rarely talk in these moments, and there are no threats or puzzles.

Apple has already revealed many of the new features coming in macOS 27 Golden Gate, the next major update for the Mac. Headline changes include an all-new Siri AI assistant, major upgrades to apps including Safari, Photos, Messages, Mail and Calendar, expanded child-safety features, design refinements and performance improvements throughout the operating system. We’ve also had the chance to see many of these features in action through the beta, with the full release now likely to be only days away.

Golden Gate continues Apple’s tradition of naming macOS releases after iconic Californian landmarks. More broadly, the update represents another step in Apple’s push to make the Mac smarter and more proactive, with greater use of Apple Intelligence across the operating system and a stronger focus on helping users complete everyday tasks more quickly.

macOS 27 will support all Macs powered by Apple silicon, marking the end of the road for Intel-based Macs. While Intel models won’t be eligible for the new operating system, Apple is expected to continue providing security updates for them for some time.

Apple made developer and public betas of macOS 27 available, with the finished version expected in September 2026. This hub covers everything you need to know about macOS 27 Golden Gate, including its new features, compatibility, beta releases and Apple Intelligence upgrades.

What’s New in macOS 27 Golden Gate at a glance

Apple

Here are the top ten new features and changes coming with macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Siri AI: A redesigned conversational Siri that can answer questions, understand personal and onscreen context, access the web and take actions across apps.

Apple Intelligence: Systemwide proofreading, smarter writing tools, improved dictation and automatic file and folder naming.

Safari upgrades: Automatic tab grouping, webpage change alerts with Notify Me, AI-generated extensions and faster, more efficient browsing.

Smarter Messages and Mail: Personalized Smart Reply, better search and syncing, contextual suggestions and improved reliability.

New Photos tools: Spatial Reframing, image expansion with Extend, improved Clean Up and better search and organisation.

More powerful built-in apps: New features for Passwords, Calendar, Notes, Preview, Freeform, Weather, Shortcuts and Image Playground.

Expanded parental controls: Ask to Browse, improved Screen Time, contact approvals and broader Communication Safety protections.

Better Mac gaming: Game Porting Toolkit 4 promises significant performance and compatibility improvements for Windows games.

Refined Liquid Glass design: Better readability and consistency, adjustable transparency, cleaner Finder windows and improved iPhone Mirroring.

Faster macOS performance: Quicker app launches, Spotlight, AirDrop and networking, plus improved external-display, Thunderbolt and Bluetooth support.

ChatGPT for Mac now includes an Apple Messages plugin

The new Apple Messages plugin lets ChatGPT read and search chats on a Mac, and prepare and send messages.

OpenAI says it is available across all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, with support in both ChatGPT Work and Codex.

That access raises privacy and control questions, so OpenAI stresses that sending remains gated by user approval under the default settings.

Users should take care before granting persistent approval. OpenAI’s plugin guide details the risks and how to revoke access.

It also lists a known issue involving tasks that disable approval prompts: “If your task is set to Full access or otherwise disables approval prompts, Apple Messages may be unable to show the confirmation needed to send. Switch to Ask for approval or Approve for me and try again.”

How OpenAI’s Messages plugin works on the Mac

OpenAI explains that the optional Messages plugin runs locally on the Mac. Like other ChatGPT/Codex features including Computer Use, it relies on macOS system technologies like AppleScript and Accessibility.

The optional Messages plugin is not like the sketchy server-related hacks that try to bring iMessage functionality to Android. It’s simply using files on your Mac with your permission when prompted.

And unlike Siri AI, it doesn’t rely on an index of content from Messages. ChatGPT for Mac only uses the data when directed and with permission.

As you can see below, once enabled by the user, ChatGPT is super clear in what it does with messages, especially sending on your behalf when asked.

For these reasons, it shouldn’t be a privacy concern for Apple. The data exists as files on your Mac, and you need to give ChatGPT permission to work with the files. OpenAI also isn’t the only AI company to develop similar tools. It’s just a benefit of the Mac being a more capable operating system than mobile platforms.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

articles.title: After a massive 2021 office expansion, Bungie is now trying to sublease its 211,000 square foot headquarters
articles.subtitle: Bungie says it "will continue to maintain a physical office presence in Bellevue."
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
In 2021, as studio CEO Pete Parsons cited the company's recent "tremendous growth and opportunity," Bungie announced its plans for a massive expansion to its Bellevue, Washington headquarters. The campus embiggening, which internal sources have reportedly described as costing "hundreds of millions" of dollars, more than doubled the size of Bungie's offices from 84,000 square feet to just under 211,000.

Now, after five and a half years of spending sprees, publisher acquisitions, stumbling product launches, project cancellations, and repeated mass layoffs, Bungie appears to be seeking subletters for the goliath game development headquarters it's no longer capable of filling.

According to a 10-page leasing brochure reviewed by The Game Post, Bungie is seeking interested renters to sublease its expansive headquarters, listing its 210,984 square feet as a "turn-key" production facility. In addition to expected office fixtures, the listing also features a dedicated lobby, gym and exercise facilities (including a rock climbing wall), a motion-capture studio, a cafe, catering space, and a private exterior patio.

While the brochure didn't directly identify the studio, a statement provided to press verified that Bungie was actively pursuing a sublease.

"Bungie is exploring options to sublease its campus in Bellevue, Washington. The studio transitioned to a digital-first model several years ago, and this move reflects the team's evolving workplace needs and the effectiveness of its remote collaboration," Bungie said. "Bungie will continue to maintain a physical office presence in Bellevue."

Bungie formally adopted remote work eligibility for most of its roles in 2022, following the studio's shift to work-from-home development during the COVID-19 lockdown years—effectively defeating the purpose of its office expansion due to circumstances that would have been impossible to predict during its early planning stages.

Bungie wasn't the only games company to make ill-fated investments during the height of the pandemic: Analysts have repeatedly cited overly-ambitious expansions and acquisitions—propelled by the COVID era's low interests rates and explosion of at-home entertainment revenue—as one of the driving forces behind the games industry's brutal cost-cutting in the years that followed.

Bungie's overextension, however, was particularly drastic. After Sony purchased the studio for $3.6 billion in 2022, Bungie leadership embarked on a rampant hiring spree, adding hundreds of developers to the payroll to fill out development teams for a swath of simultaneous incubation projects—projects that would prove unsustainable as the impact of Covid waned and revenues started to tumble across the industry.

A mass layoff followed in October 2023, affecting roughly 100 employees. The next round cut 220 developers in July 2024 as fallout from Bungie leadership having reportedly "overstated their studio’s financial prospects to Sony," leading to a dire enough fiscal outlook that even the success of Destiny 2's Final Shape expansion couldn't salvage it.

As Sony intensified its oversight amidst the mounting turmoil, Bungie's leadership began to abandon ship, culminating with Pete Parsons departing the studio in 2025—presumably in one of his vintage collector cars.

Bungie staff ultimately suffered another sweeping layoff in June 2026, with most of the Destiny team losing their jobs in the aftermath of Destiny 2's end of live service. At peak employment, Bungie's staff numbered over 1,600; in July 2024, Parsons said the studio numbered around 850. The WARN notice issued for this June's layoff indicated at least 292 jobs were affected.

In other words, if all of Bungie's remaining employees gathered in its office, there would be fewer than 600 people to fill its 211,000 square feet.

If you're interested, the master lease runs through September 30, 2035.
